areasOfOperation.title: Preflight Preparation
areasOfOperation.groundingNotes: Commercial pilot privileges (14 CFR 61.133): may act as PIC of aircraft for compensation or hire; may act as SIC. Limitations: cannot act as PIC of aircraft for compensation or hire carrying passengers or property on cross-country flights over 50 NM or at night unless instrument rated (14 CFR 61.133(b)). Commercial certificate requires 250 hours total time including: 100 hours in powered aircraft, 100 hours PIC, 50 hours XC PIC, 10 hours instrument (5 in airplanes), 10 hours in complex/TAA aircraft. Complex aircraft: retractable gear, flaps, and controllable-pitch propeller. High-performance aircraft: more than 200 HP. Commercial pilot must hold at least a third-class medical. Drug and alcohol regulations: 14 CFR 91.17 — 8 hours bottle-to-throttle, 0.04 BAC limit.

areasOfOperation.title: Takeoffs, Landings, and Go-Arounds
areasOfOperation.groundingNotes: TODO: Add grounding notes — commercial standards are tighter than Private: short-field touchdown within 200 ft of aiming point (vs 400 ft Private), precision approaches. Power-off 180° accuracy approach: engine at idle abeam touchdown point, land within 200 ft of a designated point. Retractable gear: verify gear DOWN before landing; GUMP check on final. If gear-up landing occurs — major incident. Normal landing: touch down in first third of runway.

areasOfOperation.title: Performance Maneuvers
areasOfOperation.groundingNotes: Chandelle: 180° climbing turn to just above stall speed; maximum pitch attitude reached at 90° of turn and held; rollout completed at 180° exactly as aircraft reaches minimum controllable airspeed. Lazy Eight: symmetrical maneuver across two 180° turns — pitch and bank increase together to 45° bank / maximum pitch at 45° of turn, then decrease to level at 90°, then repeat in opposite direction; altitude, airspeed, and heading should match at each 90° point. Both maneuvers demonstrate mastery of aircraft control at varying airspeeds and demonstrate coordination. Common errors: chandelle — not reaching max pitch at 90°; lazy eight — not coordinating bank and pitch changes together.

areasOfOperation.title: Ground Reference Maneuvers
areasOfOperation.groundingNotes: Eights on pylons (pylon eights): altitude selected so pivotal altitude formula is satisfied: altitude (ft) = groundspeed (kt)² ÷ 11.3. At pivotal altitude, the wingtip appears to pivot on the pylon. If pylon appears to move forward, you are too high — descend. If pylon appears to move back, you are too low — climb. Unlike other ground reference maneuvers, bank is NOT adjusted for wind during eights on pylons — altitude is the control. Pylon spacing should allow approximately 3 to 5 seconds of straight flight between pylons.

areasOfOperation.title: Slow Flight and Stalls
areasOfOperation.groundingNotes: Left-turning tendencies still apply — RIGHT RUDDER required during slow flight and stalls. Commercial ACS requires stall recognition and recovery before full stall buffet where possible. Accelerated stalls: occur at higher-than-normal airspeed due to increased load factor (e.g., steep turn); load factor at 60° bank = 2G, stall speed increases by 41% (square root of load factor). Secondary stall: occurs when recovery from first stall is premature — student pulls back before airspeed builds sufficiently. Cross-control stall: most dangerous — occurs in low, slow, uncoordinated turn (base-to-final); outside wing stalls first causing snap roll toward ground; avoid by maintaining coordinated flight in the pattern.

areasOfOperation.title: High-Altitude Operations
areasOfOperation.groundingNotes: Pressurization systems maintain cabin altitude typically at 6000–8000 ft regardless of flight altitude. Cabin differential pressure: the difference between cabin pressure and outside air pressure. At cabin altitude 8000 ft, oxygen not required but recommended. At cabin altitude above 12,500 ft: crew must use supplemental O2 after 30 minutes. Above 14,000 ft cabin altitude: crew must use O2 continuously. Above 15,000 ft cabin altitude: passengers must be provided O2. Rapid decompression: don oxygen mask immediately (useful consciousness at 30,000 ft is only 15-30 seconds without O2). Emergency descent: deploy oxygen, establish emergency descent, squawk 7700, declare emergency with ATC, plan for landing. High-density altitude effects: reduced engine power, reduced prop efficiency, reduced lift — all performance numbers degrade.
